title: Continuity routing scenarios and operational playbook
content:
Purpose
This note collects practical routing/control-plane patterns we can adopt to deliver graceful degradation across Hosted/Dedicated/Private deployments. It emphasizes multi-region spillover, prioritized capacity tiers, and model-variant hedging that preserves functional correctness while protecting latency SLOs and customer SLAs.

Key ideas (one-liner)
- Treat capacity as an explicit, accountable resource (resilience budget).
- Prefer deterministic, explainable fallbacks over opaque load-shedding.
- Route by latency/cost/priority vectors; fall back along predefined "continuity chains" of models and regions.

Design goals
- Keep p95 latency within SLO where possible; provide transparent degradations when not.
- Prioritize high-value tenants and interactive flows for scarce capacity.
- Automatic but auditable decisions: every fallback step is logged and reversible.
- Sane defaults for self-serve customers, tunable for enterprise.

Core components we require
1) Continuity policy store (control-plane):
   - Small JSON/YAML DSL per tenant+route describing priority vectors, fallback chain, and cost/latency sensitivity.
   - Versioned, feature-flagged, and rollout-capable.
2) Capacity ledger & token broker:
   - Per-region, per-pool counters representing reserved/burst/best-effort buckets.
   - Lease tokens issued to frontends for the lifetime of a request to avoid race conditions.
3) Model-family registry:
   - Metadata for each model variant: cost-per-token, quantization, expected latency distribution, compatibility score with canonical model.
4) Router + Decision engine (at edge/proxy):
   - Evaluates policy + capacity + recent telemetry to pick target region/model.
   - Supports speculative hedging and parallel requests when configured.
5) Observability hooks:
   - Per-request annotation of chosen path (region, pool, model variant, reason code).
   - Aggregated metrics: fallback rate, spillover rate, priority denial rate, cost delta.

Routing policy primitives (DSL sketch)
- priority: numeric (0..100) per route; higher wins for preemption.
- continuity_chain: ordered list of model families (e.g., [gptx-1, gptx-1-quant, gptx-1-distill, embed-lite])
- region_preference: ordered list with soft/strict flags (soft allows spillover beyond list)
- latency_target_ms: desired p95 for route
- cost_sensitivity: low|medium|high (instructs how aggressive we are at switching to cheaper variants)
- degrade_mode: degrade|reject|queue (default degrade)

Decision flow (per request)
1) Authenticate + load tenant policy.
2) Evaluate local pool capacity for preferred region. If capacity token available and predicted latency meets latency_target, route locally.
3) If not available, check continuity_chain next variant in same region (quantized/distilled). Test compatibility: tokenization/IO shapes.
4) If same-region alternatives exhausted, consult regional spillover ranking: attempt next region if network latency budget allows (per-route).
5) If spillover denied (latency or policy), apply degradation behavior: reduce response length, switch to cached response, fall back to embedding-only rerank, or finally return structured error with graceful suggestion.
6) Always annotate and emit metric and tenant event for auditing.

Tiered capacity model (terms)
- Reserved: pre-allocated capacity for enterprise commitments. Hard guarantee for route-level throughput.
- Baseline: low-priority committed capacity for sustained workloads.
- Burst: ephemeral pool for short spikes; best-effort.
- Overflow/best-effort: cheap, opportunistic capacity (may use lower-performing hardware or spot pools).
- Emergency: automatic throttling and denial when all else fails.

Preemption and reservations
- Priority vectors allow preemption: a higher-priority request can consume tokens from Burst if policy permits; Reserved tokens are never preempted for that tenant.
- Preemption policy must be auditable and bounded (max preempted-per-minute).

Model variant guidance (practical mappings)
- Canonical (full): high-fidelity model, higher cost. Use when latency budget permits and tenant priority high.
- Quantized: 8-bit/4-bit variant with similar outputs for most prompts; fallback first for capacity stress.
- Distill/smaller family: lower token-cost and often lower quality; best reserved for bulk/async workloads.
- Response-shrinking: same model family but force lower max_tokens / shorter context to reduce compute.
- Cached/semantic fallback: for repeated queries, return cached or embedding-based nearest response if confidence high.

Regional spillover heuristics
- Soft spillover: prefer same continent/closest region if p95 increase <= X ms (configurable per route). Default X = 80ms for interactive flows.
- Cold-start avoidance: prefer variants in region where KV/caches warmed.
- Regulatory exclusions: policy flags per tenant can disable cross-border spillover.
- Cost-aware spillover: annotates cost delta for downstream billing transparency.

Graceful degradation examples (play scenarios)
- Scenario A: sudden 3x request spike in us-west, reserved capacity saturated.
   - Step 1: fill Burst tokens in us-west.
   - Step 2: concurrently enable quantized variant in us-west for lower-priority routes.
   - Step 3: for interactive high-priority tenants, allow soft spillover to us-central if latency penalty < 60ms.
   - Step 4: start shedding best-effort background jobs (queue/raise backpressure) and notify SRE channel.
- Scenario B: entire region OOMs (hardware failure)
   - Step 1: global router marks region unhealthy, immediate spillover to next region listing for all affected tenants.
   - Step 2: throttle long-tail batch workloads platform-wide to free capacity for interactive flows.
   - Step 3: enable emergency reduced-length policy for all non-enterprise tenants.

Operational playbook (on-call)
- Triage checklist: check region health, capacity ledger, recent rollout flags, and model registry changes.
- Quick mitigations: open more Burst capacity if pool healthy; disable non-critical canaries; toggle degrade_mode to "queue" for long-running batches.
- Customer comms: use templated messages with per-tenant annotations about chosen fallback (model/region) and expected resolution ETA.

Testing and validation
- Chaos scenarios: region-autoscaling-fail, model-variant-unavailability, token-broker-deadlock.
- Canary experiments: slow rollout of new continuity policy to small tenant cohort; monitor fallback-rate and latency delta.
- Regression tests: ensure output compatibility across model-variants for critical prompt-templates (evaluate using our eval suite).

Metrics to instrument (minimum)
- fallback_rate_by_route (ratio)
- spillover_rate_by_region (count)
- per-tenant_priority_denials (count & reason)
- latency_delta_after_fallback (ms)
- cost_delta_after_fallback ($)
- continuity_policy_mismatch_events (count)

Open questions / trade-offs
- How aggressive should cross-region spillover be for low-latency interactive apps? (default conservative, allow per-route override)
- Do we expose continuity policy editing to self-serve customers? (risk: accidental global preemption)
- How to balance caching warmup vs. warm expensive hardware across regions?

Immediate next steps (quarter roadmap items)
- Build minimal Continuity DSL + UI in Console (MVP) for reserved customers.
- Implement token-broker prototype with lease semantics (safety-first).
- Start an infra chaos suite for regional spillover and model-family failover.
- Draft customer-facing docs that explain what "graceful degradation" will look like in invoices and SLAs.

Notes to reviewers
- This is a working doc: please add concrete tenant examples and edge cases in inline comments.
- We should align terms (Burst vs. Baseline) with billing language before GA.

TODO (short)

- Link sample continuity policies for top 10 customers.
- Author SRE runbooks for each failure class.
